name: Insurance
blurb: Underwriting, claims triage, and fraud detection under active regulator supervision, with NAIC, AM Best, and the Evident insurance index.

points.desc: The NAIC model bulletin on insurers' use of AI - adopted by a growing majority of states - is the operative US governance document for the sector.
points.name: NAIC set the supervisory frame

points.desc: Outside-in benchmarking of the major global insurers on AI talent, innovation, leadership, and transparency - the sector's comparative maturity scoreboard.
points.name: The Evident AI Index benchmarks insurers

points.desc: The National Association of Insurance Commissioners sets the model-governance and algorithmic-fairness expectations US carriers answer to - the binding layer over underwriting AI.
points.name: NAIC governs the algorithms

points.desc: The insurance rating agency evaluates innovation and digital maturity as part of its assessments - technology capability reaching credit opinion.
points.name: AM Best rates innovation capability

reading.body:
The operative constraint on insurance AI is regulatory: the NAIC model bulletin, adopted by a growing majority of states, sets algorithmic-fairness expectations for underwriting, claims triage, and fraud detection.

The pattern is supervision plus external benchmarking. NAIC appears twice, as the source of the model bulletin and as the body setting model-governance expectations, which makes it the binding layer over underwriting AI. AM Best folds innovation and digital maturity into credit opinion, and the Evident AI Index scores insurers on talent, innovation, leadership, and transparency. Together these measure governance and capability, not model output.

The data does not cover compute, data center capacity, or grid constraints, so it cannot support claims about infrastructure limits on insurance AI. It also gives no adoption counts or performance figures beyond the statement that a growing majority of states have adopted the bulletin. What it establishes is that the sector's AI deployments are named and supervised, with fairness expectations attached to the three core use cases.

summary: Underwriting, claims triage, and fraud detection are the deployments regulators are actively supervising.
